LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Can — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: you will show the grown-up one thing you can do, then name it: “I can hop”, and your child will meet “can” in a real sentence, “I can jump.” By the end, “can” should be a word they know at a glance.

What is this?

“Can” is a small helping word that links who with what or how. On this card, a boy flexes his arm to show how strong he is, with the word printed in big, clear letters underneath.

What does it mean?

“Can” is a helper word: it links the person doing something to what they are, do or did, as in “I can jump.”

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to recognise “can” at a glance, say it clearly, and begin to hear it in the stories you read together. Good hunting grounds: proud moments: “I can do it”, “I can tie my shoe”.

Why this matters

Helper words like “can” cannot be drawn as a simple picture, so they are best learned by seeing them again and again in sentences.

What it teaches

Sentence sense, letter-sound matching on irregular spellings and fluent reading of short sentences.

Words to learn

wordreadsentence

Say this to your child

“Look at this card. It says ‘can’. I can jump. Now you say ‘can’. Well done!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and read “can” clearly, running your finger under the letters. Let your child say it back, twice.
  2. Look at the picture together: a boy flexes his arm to show how strong he is. Ask what is happening, then link the picture to the word.
  3. Play one tiny game: show the grown-up one thing you can do, then name it: “I can hop”. Read the word one last time and stop while it is still fun.

Look closer at the picture

Point to the word first, then to the picture. Cover the picture with your hand and read the word; lift your hand to check. Then let your child trace the first letter with one finger.

Ask your child

“What does the card say?” “Can you say it in a sentence?” “Who is doing something in the picture?” — answered with a read-aloud and a short sentence of their own.

What your child can say or do

Expect your child to read “can” aloud before sounding it out, and to use it in everyday sentences like “I can jump.”

Out in the real world

Watch for “can” here: proud moments: “I can do it”, “I can tie my shoe”. Every sighting is a free practice round: point, say it, move on.

Try it together

Show the grown-up one thing you can do, then name it: “I can hop”. Finish by saying “can” one more time.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, hold up the card without saying a word. If your child reads “can” straight away, the word has arrived; if not, play the game once more and try again the day after.

Parent tips

Keep it short: five minutes is plenty. Add “can” to the pile only when the cards your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the Can flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).
